extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students in real analysis and instructors assigning Rudin-style problem sets
extracted.subtask_description: Instructor's annotated problem list and hints for exercises from Rudin (chapters on differentiation, Taylor, and the Riemann(-Stieltjes) integral). Gives what students should prove, which parts are essential, suggested prerequisites, and grading-relevant remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Part (c) limit-of-sequence requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Part (c) ends by asking you to prove 'that x = lim xn where x1 is an arbitrary real number' — show that for every real number x1, if one defines x2 etc. using that relation, then x = lim xn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret the instruction as: your proof must work for an arbitrary initial x1 (not just some special choice). Make explicit the dependence on x1 and prove convergence of the sequence to x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Part (d) treated as suggestion unless specified
rubrics_metrics.description: For part (d), it is hard to see what sort of answer one could be expected to hand in and have graded; so unless the instructor gives precise instructions on that count, it is probably best to regard this part merely as a suggestion on how to get intuition on the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to write up part (d) as a formal graded solution unless the instructor explicitly asks for a precise deliverable; treat it as exploratory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do difference-quotients approach f'
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: Do difference-quotients (f(βn) – f(αn)) / (βn – αn) approach f' ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider sequences αn, βn approaching a point and compare the difference quotients to the derivative; check hypotheses (continuity, differentiability) and dependence on how αn,βn approach the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique fixed points of differentiable functions R→R
rubrics_metrics.description: Study uniqueness of fixed points for differentiable functions R → R (exercise reference 5: R22 / related exercises).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use derivative information (e.g., contraction mapping / mean value theorem) to deduce uniqueness or multiplicity of fixed points; refer to preceding exercises about iterative sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify nontrivial parts after a Hint
rubrics_metrics.description: Note that the sentences after the Hint are a nontrivial part of the exercise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an exercise contains a Hint followed by extra sentences, those sentences are not optional commentary — include them in your solution and justify any assertions they contain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three fixed points of (x^3 + 1) / 3
rubrics_metrics.description: Find the three fixed points of the map x ↦ (x^3 + 1)/3 and analyze their nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate to R22 and R23; check stability/attractiveness via derivatives and consider iteration sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite review before tackling some exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should look over specified earlier exercises (e.g., 3: R16, 3: R17 and 5: R22) before attempting later problems such as 5: R24.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do preparatory reading of referenced exercises; you may not need to have fully solved them but should understand their statements and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Root-finding algorithms: convergence rate contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why some root-finding algorithms converge much faster than others (5: R24).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare iteration maps, local error propagation, and use Taylor expansions / derivative bounds; refer to preceding Newton-method exercises for techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: If |f'| ≤ A|f| then f can't escape from 0
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove that if |f'(x)| ≤ A |f(x)| on an interval then f cannot 'escape' from 0 (exercise 5: R26).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exercise is presented in contrapositive form: show that if f ever becomes nonzero then f' moves away from zero at most at a rate proportional to f. Rudin's hint is correct but messy; consider using supremum-based contradiction: let c = sup{x ∈ [a,b] : f(t)=0 for all t∈[a,x]} and derive contradiction for d∈[c,b] with d < c + 1/A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply 5:R26 to differential equations uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the previous result to study differential equations with unique and nonunique solutions (5: R27).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sentences after the Hint are important — include them. Use the bound on |f'| in analyzing the behavior of solutions and uniqueness via Gronwall-type arguments or comparison estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: True/False question answering precision
rubrics_metrics.description: When listing answers to True/False questions (examples: 4.7, 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 5.4, ...), state each part and justify your answer where required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide brief but correct explanations for each True/False choice; the document lists answer keys but assignment may require justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strictly increasing functions characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Which differentiable functions are strictly increasing? Show necessary and sufficient derivative conditions (5.2:1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove: a continuous f on [a,b] differentiable on (a,b) is strictly increasing iff (i) f'≥0 on (a,b) and (ii) for every p<q there exists r∈(p,q) with f'(r)>0 (or equivalently: f'≥0 and f' not identically zero on any subinterval). Use the mean value theorem for implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fake counterexample caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware of fake counterexamples to Theorem 5.9 (exercise 5.2:2): sketch and explain why proposed counterexamples fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze details carefully (especially at boundary/special points) and check hypotheses of the theorem to see why the counterexample does not satisfy them or why the theorem still applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions as difference of two increasing functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine which functions can be written as g1 − g2 with g1,g2 increasing (5.2:3 parts a-c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show constructive decompositions when derivative has only finitely many zeros (part a). Show unbounded functions on [a,b] cannot be so written (part b). For subtler cases (c) build examples similar to Rudin's Example 5.6(b) and analyze zero-sets and summation constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean-value theorem with infinite endpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove a version of the mean-value theorem when endpoints may be infinite: if lim_{x→a} f(x)=lim_{x→b} f(x) exist and are equal then there exists c with f'(c)=0 (5.2:4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Rudin's conventions that limits referred to are finite real numbers. Adapt standard proof of Rolle's theorem to possibly unbounded intervals by compactification or argument on large finite subintervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for existence of one-sided limit from bounded derivative
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that if f is differentiable on (a,b) and f' is bounded then lim_{x→a} f(x) exists (5.2:5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use uniform continuity consequences of bounded derivative on (a,b) and apply limit existence lemmas (e.g., 4.1:3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on discontinuities of f'
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises show limitations on where or how f' can be discontinuous (Section 5.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use connectivity/mean-value theorems and left/right limit considerations; e.g., demonstrate impossibility of certain infinite one-sided limits of f' at interior points.

rubrics_metrics.name: L'Hospital variants and lim sup / lim inf versions
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapt proofs of L'Hospital's rule to get lim sup/lim inf versions and to extend to complex-valued or vector-valued functions when appropriate hypotheses hold (5.4:1, 5.7:2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the proof structure of Theorem 5.13, replacing exact limits by lim sup/lim inf manipulations and apply componentwise arguments for vector/complex cases; note extra hypotheses needed (e.g., ratios of real/imaginary parts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute higher derivatives by single limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute second derivatives using just one limit operation where possible (5: R11).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Rudin's hint ordering; produce examples and be mindful of manipulations that avoid nested limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of x^a sin(|x|^{−c}) and variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze differentiability and higher-order behavior for functions like x^a sin(|x|^{−c}) (5: R13 and continuations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scaling, oscillation analysis near 0, and differentiation rules; refer to earlier comments about what may be assumed for these exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convexity and second derivative relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Relate convexity of a function to sign/behavior of f'' (5: R14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply definitions of convexity and second derivative tests; recall earlier Exercise 4:R23 for convex function definition references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smooth functions with arbitrary zero-sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct smooth functions whose zero-sets match prescribed sets and discuss derivatives of all orders (5: R21).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parts up to a point are rated d:4; the last phrase concerning derivatives of all orders is more difficult — consider starting with exercise 5.6:1 for techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newton's method basics and notation clarifications
rubrics_metrics.description: In Rudin's statement 'f'(x) ≥ δ > 0 [...] for all x ∈ [a,b]' mean 'there exists δ > 0 such that f'(x) ≥ δ for all x ∈ [a,b]'; similar clarifications for bounds on f'' (5: R25).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using Rudin's hypotheses, rephrase ambiguous quantified statements into standard 'there exists δ > 0 such that for all x...' form. For part (a) show inductively given inequalities for iterates xn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bell-shaped curves and their higher derivatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze zeros of higher derivatives for bell-shaped functions like 1/(x^2+1), 1/(x^4+1), e^{−x^2} and show nth derivative has at least n zeros (5.5:1 parts a-c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use known properties of these functions, Rolle's theorem, and comparison with polynomials for counting zeros; sketch graphs to build intuition and then formalize with derivative sign-counting and degree arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounded derivative implies uniform continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Show (a) if f' is bounded then f is uniformly continuous; (b) give example where f is uniformly continuous but f' unbounded; (c) if twice differentiable and second derivative bounded then first derivative must be bounded or provide consequences (5.5:2 parts a-c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mean value theorem for (a). For (b) construct functions that wiggle more and more while remaining uniformly continuous (hint toward examples). For (c) show constraints on second derivative growth and implications for uniform continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lagrange interpolation and remainder formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove existence of polynomial of degree ≤ n agreeing with f at n+1 points, build Lagrange interpolation polynomial q and derive remainder E in terms of nth derivative of f (5.5:3 parts a-d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use constructive addition of scalar multiples of (x − x0)...(x − xi−1) to match values iteratively; take nth derivative of constructed polynomial and apply part (a) to bound interpolation error when f^{(n)} is bounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taylor series vs function equality counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a C^∞ function (e^{-1/x^2} with f(0)=0) whose Taylor polynomials at 0 converge but not to the original function (5.6:1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume needed properties of e^x; show derivatives at 0 are 0 so Taylor series vanishes but function not identically zero. Work through parts (a)-(e) to justify differentiability and behavior of derivatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lagrange interpolation with multiplicities
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalize Lagrange interpolation to points with multiplicity: if f has zeros of multiplicity m_i at x_i and Σ m_i = n, prove analogs of 5.5:3 and recover Taylor's theorem as a special case (5.6:2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define multiplicity precisely and adapt remainder arguments taking into account multiple vanishing derivatives at nodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taylor theorem bounds and applications to Newton method
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Taylor's theorem with remainder to derive bounds relating f, f', and f'' and obtain convergence estimates for Newton's method (5: R15, R16, R17, R18, and 5:R25 parts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match variables carefully when applying the theorem in iterative contexts; check exponents (note a display where exponent is 2^n not 2_n) and interpret geometric meanings when asked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vector-valued differentiation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend scalar differentiation results to vector-valued functions: uniform differentiability, product rules with inner products, L'Hospital-type results for R^k-valued functions (5.7: various).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply componentwise arguments and use inner product properties. For L'Hospital generalization, either treat components separately or add extra hypotheses (e.g., ratios of Re/Im limits in complex case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disconnected derivative ranges and vector corollary
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct differentiable f:[a,b]→R whose derivative values set {f'(x) | x∈[a,b]} is not connected; but show corollary that for vector-valued f:[a,b]→R^k the derivative has no simple discontinuities (5.7:3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit counterexample for scalar case. For vector case, apply componentwise corollary of Theorem 5.12 to conclude restrictions on derivative discontinuities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann integral: single-point exceptions integrate to zero
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove that a function which is zero except at one point c∈(a,b) is Riemann integrable and has integral zero (6.1:1 and 6:R1 analogue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use partitions that avoid the single point and bound the contribution of the single-point value via arbitrarily small intervals around c.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann-Stieltjes integrability depends on continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that a function f is Riemann-Stieltjes integrable with respect to every increasing α iff f is continuous (exercise derived from 6:R3 parts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study integrals against step-functions with different continuity choices at a point c and use examples to show necessity and sufficiency of continuity for integrability with respect to all increasing α.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition mesh limit definition equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Show the usual definition of Riemann integral as limit over partitions whose mesh→0 is equivalent to Rudin's upper/lower sums definition (6.2:2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove equivalence by controlling sums when refining partitions and using the fact that refining by adding points changes sums by at most 2M·||P|| when |f| ≤ M. Provide δ(ε) arguments converting partition mesh to upper-lower sum bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for Riemann-Stieltjes integrability technical equivalences
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove equivalence of symmetric integrability conditions: α∈(β) iff β∈(α) iff for every ε there is a partition P with Σ Δα_i Δβ_i < ε (6.2:1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with partitions and the definitions of Δα_i, Δβ_i; show implications both directions carefully using refinement sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious formula ∫ 1 dα = α(b) − α(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that for any increasing α on [a,b], ∫_a^b 1 dα = α(b) − α(a) (6.3:1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a direct consequence of the Riemann-Stieltjes integral definition and should be justified as part of the integral's basic properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions mostly zero have integral zero
rubrics_metrics.description: If a bounded function f on [0,1] has the property that for every ε>0 the set {x: |f(x)| ≥ ε} is finite, then f∈(α) and ∫ f dα = 0 for any continuous increasing α (6.3:2 parts a-b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use partitioning to isolate finitely many nonzero points into small intervals whose α-variation is arbitrarily small; apply to the given example that is 0 on irrationals and rational-value exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct increasing α supported on Cantor set
rubrics_metrics.description: Build an increasing function α which increases only on the Cantor set P (6.3:3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define α0 on complement segments to have specified constant values on removed middle-thirds and extend to full [0,1] customizing values on each deleted segment to accumulate all increase on Cantor set; analyze integrability consequences.
